title: Nanotube space elevator
summary: Future Technology 3. Rockets spend most of their fuel just reaching orbital speed, which is why getting to space is costly. A cable of carbon nanotubes runs from a base at sea on the equator straight up, past the height where a satellite circles once a day, to a counterweight beyond it; the Earth's spin flings the counterweight outward and keeps the cable taut. Electric climbers, powered by sunlight or a laser beamed from the ground, ride up the cable carrying payloads to orbit at the cost of electricity.

title: Resonance
summary: Push a swing in time with its own rhythm and each small push adds up until it flies high; anything that can vibrate, from a wine glass to a bridge to an electric circuit, responds hugely to pushes at its own natural frequency and hardly at all to others. Galileo described it in 1638, noting that well-timed puffs of breath could set a heavy pendulum swinging. Radios tune to one station this way, quartz watches keep time by it, and MRI scanners use it to pick out hydrogen atoms.
